Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

ALLENTOWN, Pennsylvania (CNN)  -- A federal court Thursday struck down ordinances passed by Hazleton, Pennsylvania, that were intended to limit where illegal immigrants could live and work. Last year, Hazleton passed the Illegal Immigration Relief Act Ordinance, which would have fined landlords who rented to undocumented immigrants and would have penalized companies that employed them. Under another law, tenants would have had to prove they were citizens or lawful residents, register with the city and pay for a rental permit in order to receive an occupancy permit. The ordinances were copied by other cities. The court ruled that Hazleton cannot enact any ordinances dealing with illegal immigration because they conflict with the supremacy clause of the U.S. constitution. "Hazleton, in its zeal to control the presence of a group deemed undesirable, violated the rights of such people, as well as others within the community. Since the United States Constitution protects even the disfavored, the ordinances cannot be enforced," U.S. District Judge James M. Munley wrote in the 206-page opinion. Mayor Lou Barletta, who spearheaded the opposition, said he will appeal the ruling. "This fight is far from over," he told reporters outside the courtroom. "Hazleton is not going to back down. ... We will take it all the way to the Supreme Court if we have to."  Watch mayor decry "injustice" » . Barletta drafted the act last year after "a high-profile murder, the discharge of a gun at a crowded city playground, and drug busts" allegedly involving illegal immigrants, he wrote on his Web site, www.smalltowndefenders.com. "Illegal aliens in our city create an economic burden that threatens our quality of life," he wrote. "With a growing problem and a limited budget, I could not sit back any longer and allow this to happen. I needed to act!" Hazleton's population was 23,000 in 2000. Since then, it has risen to an estimated 30,000 to 33,000, with many of the newcomers being Mexican immigrants, according to Munley. The American Civil Liberties Union of Pennsylvania was among several groups that filed the suit on behalf of Hazleton residents, landlords and business owners. The groups contended that only the federal government has the right to regulate immigration or to deprive residents of the rights to equal protection. In addition, they said, the ordinances violated state and federal housing laws. The ordinances, Munley said, "penalize landlords, tenants, employers and employees without providing them the procedural protections required by federal law, including notice and an opportunity to be heard." "Our analysis applies to illegal aliens as well as to legal residents and citizens. The United States Constitution provides due process protections to all persons," he wrote, emphasizing "all." The city exceeded its police powers by enacting unconstitutional ordinances, wrote Munley, whom President Clinton appointed to the federal bench in 1998. Barletta said he would "continue to fight for the people of this community and other cities around the country." "It's almost amusing to me that the judge would say we can't do what the federal government should be doing, when in fact the federal government is not doing their job," he told CNN's Lou Dobbs. A spokesman for the ACLU of Pennsylvania expressed satisfaction with the ruling. "Hazleton-type laws are designed to make life miserable for millions of immigrants," said Vic Walczak, legal director for the group and a lead attorney in the case. "They promote distrust of all foreigners, including those here legally, and fuel xenophobia and discrimination, especially against Latinos." Anthony D. Romero, executive director of the ACLU, added, "Political leaders, like Mayor Barletta, must stop scape-goating undocumented immigrants for all the problems we confront in our local communities." ALLENTOWN, Pennsylvania (CNN) — On Thursday, a federal court invalidated laws adopted by Hazleton, Pennsylvania, that sought to restrict where undocumented immigrants could work and reside.

In 2006, the city approved the Illegal Immigration Relief Act Ordinance. It called for fines against property owners who leased housing to undocumented immigrants and sanctions against businesses that hired them. A separate measure required renters to establish that they were U.S. citizens or legal residents, enroll with the city, and purchase a rental permit before they could obtain permission to occupy a home. Other municipalities later modeled their own laws on Hazleton’s measures.

The court concluded that Hazleton lacked the authority to pass immigration-related ordinances because they conflicted with the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution.

In his 206-page ruling, U.S. District Judge James M. Munley said the city’s determination to remove a population it considered unwelcome had infringed not only on that group’s rights but also on the rights of other community members. Because constitutional protections extend even to people who are unpopular, he wrote, the ordinances could not be enforced.

Mayor Lou Barletta, who led the campaign for the laws, announced that he would challenge the decision. Speaking to reporters outside the courthouse, he said the dispute was not finished, Hazleton would not retreat, and the city was prepared to pursue the case as far as the U.S. Supreme Court if necessary. A video showed the mayor condemning what he described as an “injustice.”

Barletta wrote on his website, www.smalltowndefenders.com, that he developed the legislation the previous year following several widely publicized incidents allegedly connected to undocumented immigrants: a murder, a gun being fired at a crowded municipal playground, and drug arrests. He argued that undocumented immigrants imposed financial costs on Hazleton and endangered residents’ quality of life. Faced with what he described as a worsening situation and a tight city budget, he said he believed he could no longer remain inactive and had to respond.

Hazleton had approximately 23,000 residents in 2000. Judge Munley said its population had since grown to an estimated 30,000 to 33,000, with Mexican immigrants accounting for many of the new arrivals.

The Pennsylvania chapter of the American Civil Liberties Union was one of several organizations that brought the lawsuit for local residents, landlords, and business owners. The plaintiffs argued that immigration regulation belongs exclusively to the federal government and that the city could not deny residents equal protection under the law. They also maintained that the ordinances violated both Pennsylvania and federal housing statutes.

Munley found that the measures punished property owners, renters, employers, and workers without giving them the procedural safeguards mandated by federal law, such as proper notice and a chance to present their case.

He stressed that the court’s reasoning covered undocumented immigrants, lawful residents, and U.S. citizens alike because the Constitution guarantees due process to every person. Munley, who was appointed to the federal judiciary by President Bill Clinton in 1998, also determined that Hazleton had gone beyond its lawful police authority by adopting unconstitutional legislation.

Barletta vowed to keep advocating for Hazleton’s residents and for communities elsewhere in the country. In an interview with CNN’s Lou Dobbs, he said he found it nearly ironic that the judge ruled the city could not take on responsibilities assigned to the federal government when, in Barletta’s view, federal authorities were failing to perform those duties.

The ACLU of Pennsylvania welcomed the decision. Vic Walczak, the organization’s legal director and one of the case’s lead lawyers, said laws modeled on Hazleton’s were intended to make everyday life intolerable for millions of immigrants. He argued that such measures encouraged suspicion toward all foreign-born people, including lawful immigrants, and intensified xenophobia and discriminatory treatment, particularly against Latinos.

ACLU Executive Director Anthony D. Romero said elected officials such as Barletta should stop blaming undocumented immigrants for every difficulty faced by local communities.

The original CNN page also included options to watch the mayor’s remarks and e-mail the story to a friend.

Hazleton, Pennsylvania, became the center of a national debate after the city enacted ordinances intended to discourage undocumented immigrants from living and working there. The measures, known collectively as the Illegal Immigration Relief Act, threatened businesses with penalties or loss of their licenses if they employed unauthorized workers. Landlords could also be fined or lose rental permits for leasing housing to undocumented immigrants. A related ordinance required tenants to register with the city, obtain occupancy permits, and provide proof of citizenship or lawful immigration status.

Residents, landlords, business owners, and civil-rights organizations challenged the laws in federal court. They argued that the ordinances encouraged discrimination, denied residents due process, and forced local officials and private citizens to make immigration determinations that properly belonged to the federal government. The challengers also maintained that the regulations could harm lawful immigrants and U.S. citizens who might be targeted because of their appearance, language, or ethnicity.

A federal judge struck down the ordinances, ruling that Hazleton had exceeded its authority. The court concluded that immigration policy is principally a federal responsibility and that municipalities cannot create their own systems for deciding who may live or work within their borders. The judge also found that the laws failed to provide adequate procedural protections before employers, landlords, or tenants could be punished.

The decision protected residents from being displaced or deprived of employment and housing through a locally administered immigration-enforcement system. It also had implications beyond Hazleton because other municipalities had adopted, or were considering, similar ordinances modeled on the city’s approach. If the ruling stood, many of those measures could also be vulnerable to constitutional challenges.

Hazleton Mayor Lou Barletta, who had strongly supported the ordinances, criticized the decision and promised to appeal. He argued that the federal government’s failure to enforce immigration laws had forced local communities to act. Civil-rights advocates, however, welcomed the ruling as an affirmation that cities cannot override federal immigration authority or deny basic constitutional protections to people within their jurisdiction.

## Federal judge strikes down Hazleton’s immigration crackdown as unconstitutional

**SCRANTON, Pennsylvania — July 26, 2007** — A federal judge on Thursday struck down a series of ordinances aimed at driving undocumented immigrants out of Hazleton, Pennsylvania, ruling that the city had intruded on the federal government’s authority over immigration and denied residents and businesses basic constitutional protections.

The ruling by U.S. District Judge James M. Munley was a major setback for Hazleton Mayor Lou Barletta, who had promoted the measures as a local response to crime, overcrowding and pressure on municipal services.

Hazleton’s Illegal Immigration Relief Act sought to punish employers who hired unauthorized immigrants and landlords who rented housing to them. A companion rental-registration ordinance required tenants to obtain occupancy permits and provide information about their immigration status.

After a nine-day trial, Munley permanently blocked the city from enforcing the laws.

“The genius of our Constitution is that it provides rights even to those who evoke the least sympathy from the general public,” Munley wrote in his 206-page decision. “In that way, all in this nation can be confident of equal justice under its laws.”

### Judge: City cannot create its own immigration system

Munley concluded that Hazleton’s ordinances conflicted with federal immigration law and therefore violated the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause, which makes federal law controlling when state or local measures interfere with national policy.

“Whatever frustrations officials of the City of Hazleton may feel about the current state of federal immigration enforcement,” Munley wrote, “the nature of the political system in the United States prohibits the City from enacting ordinances that disrupt a carefully drawn federal statutory scheme.”

The judge found that Congress had already established detailed procedures governing the employment of unauthorized immigrants, including systems for verifying work eligibility and penalties for employers. Hazleton could not impose its own licensing sanctions using different standards and procedures, he ruled.

Munley also said the housing provisions effectively required city officials and landlords to make immigration determinations that federal law assigns to federal authorities. The ordinances offered inadequate notice and too little opportunity for tenants, landlords and employers to challenge adverse decisions, violating the Due Process Clause of the 14th Amendment.

The court rejected the city’s argument that the measures were merely licensing and public-safety regulations.

### Barletta vows to continue the fight

Barletta, who later became a member of Congress, expressed disappointment and said Hazleton would appeal.

“This fight is far from over,” the mayor said after the ruling.

Barletta argued that smaller cities had been left to absorb the effects of illegal immigration while Washington failed to enforce federal law. He maintained that Hazleton’s measures targeted unlawful conduct rather than any racial or ethnic group.

The mayor had linked the ordinances to a period of rapid demographic change in the former coal-mining city, including the growth of its Latino population. He also pointed to high-profile crimes allegedly involving undocumented immigrants as evidence that local action was necessary.

Opponents disputed those claims, saying the city had not demonstrated a direct connection between undocumented immigration and higher crime. They argued that the laws encouraged landlords and employers to discriminate against anyone perceived as foreign, including U.S. citizens and legal immigrants.

### ACLU calls decision a sweeping victory

The lawsuit, *Lozano v. City of Hazleton*, was brought by Latino residents, landlords and business owners. Their legal team included the American Civil Liberties Union, the ACLU of Pennsylvania, the Puerto Rican Legal Defense and Education Fund and private attorneys.

ACLU of Pennsylvania legal director Witold Walczak described the decision as “a complete victory” for the plaintiffs and Hazleton residents.

ACLU attorneys said the ruling confirmed that municipalities cannot establish separate immigration-enforcement regimes or deprive people of housing and employment through abbreviated local proceedings. Omar Jadwat of the ACLU Immigrants’ Rights Project called the decision “a ringing affirmation of the rights of all people in this country, regardless of their immigration status.”

Civil-rights advocates said Hazleton’s ordinances had already generated fear among Latino residents, some of whom moved away or closed businesses while the legal challenge was pending. Witnesses at trial testified that even citizens and lawful immigrants could be harmed if employers or landlords acted on accents, surnames or appearance rather than risk losing city permits.

### National implications

The case was closely watched because Hazleton had become a model for similar ordinances considered by municipalities around the country. Supporters called those measures necessary responses to federal inaction; opponents described them as an unconstitutional patchwork that threatened civil rights and complicated the federal immigration system.

Munley’s ruling did not say local governments were powerless to enforce ordinary housing, employment or public-safety laws. Instead, it drew a distinction between generally applicable local regulation and measures that make immigration status the basis for penalties.

“The United States Constitution provides that the federal government has authority over immigration,” the decision said in substance, and local frustration could not override that allocation of power.

Hazleton appealed the ruling. The litigation continued for years and ultimately produced additional appellate decisions, but Munley’s 2007 judgment became an early and influential rejection of municipal efforts to create local immigration-enforcement systems.
